name: ATTINY85-20PU
title: ATtiny25/45/85 8-bit AVR microcontrollers with 2/4/8 Kbytes in-system programmable Flash
summary: An 8-pin 8-bit AVR RISC microcontroller family with 2, 4 or 8 Kbytes of Flash and 128, 256 or 512 bytes each of EEPROM and SRAM; the ATtiny85-20PU is the 8 Kbyte member in an 8-pin PDIP, rated 2.7 V to 5.5 V and up to 20 MHz at 4.5 V to 5.5 V. Six I/O lines carry an 8-bit timer with two PWM outputs, an 8-bit high-speed timer clocked up to 64 MHz from an on-chip PLL with dead-time generation, a USI for SPI- or TWI-style serial links, a 10-bit ADC with differential gain stages and a temperature sensor, and an analog comparator. Idle, ADC Noise Reduction and Power-down sleep modes, a calibrated 8 MHz RC oscillator, brown-out detection and a watchdog with its own 128 kHz oscillator round it out.
key_figures: 8-bit AVR RISC, 120 instructions, 32 x 8 working registers, up to 1 MIPS per MHz
8 Kbytes Flash, 512 bytes EEPROM, 512 bytes SRAM
2.7 V to 5.5 V (ATtiny25/45/85); 1.8 V to 5.5 V (V parts)
10-bit, 4 single-ended channels, 2 differential pairs with 1x or 20x gain, temperature sensor

circuits.title: External clock drive configuration
circuits.description: A clock from outside the chip drives CLKI on PB3, referenced to the chip's ground. CKSEL = 0000 selects it, and PB4 is then left free as an I/O.
notes: Frequency steps above 2% from one cycle to the next are not allowed; keep the part in reset through bigger changes.

circuits.title: Crystal oscillator connections
circuits.description: A quartz crystal or ceramic resonator between XTAL1 (PB3) and XTAL2 (PB4), each pin loaded by a capacitor to ground. C1 equals C2; 12 pF to 22 pF suits crystals of 0.9 MHz and up, and a resonator uses its vendor's values. A 32.768 kHz watch crystal on the low-frequency oscillator uses the same two pins, with 16 pF on XTAL1 and 6 pF on XTAL2 built in.

circuits.title: debugWIRE setup
circuits.description: The target runs from a 1.8-5.5 V supply with GND to ground. The debugger's single dW line goes straight to the RESET pin (PB5), which carries the bidirectional debug traffic once DWEN is programmed.
notes: A pull-up on dW, if used, is 10 kΩ to 20 kΩ; no capacitor or other reset source may be on the line.

circuits.title: Serial programming and verify
circuits.description: In-system programming over SPI. The programmer drives MOSI into PB0, SCK into PB2 and RESET (PB5) low, and reads MISO from PB1. VCC is 1.8-5.5 V. With the internal oscillator no clock is needed on CLKI.
notes: A clock source on CLKI (PB3) is needed only when the fuses select an external clock.

circuits.title: High-voltage serial programming
circuits.description: The programmer raises RESET (PB5) to 11.5-12.5 V with VCC at 4.5-5.5 V, clocks SCI into PB3, sends data on SDI (PB0) and instructions on SII (PB1), and reads SDO from PB2.

operation.text: PB5 to PB0 form a 6-bit bidirectional port. Each bit has its own selectable pull-up; the output stages sink and source equally well. A pin set as input with its pull-up on sources current when held low from outside. All port pins go tri-state as soon as a reset starts, with or without a running clock.

Holding RESET low longer than the minimum pulse width resets the part even with no clock, provided the pin has not been turned into an I/O; shorter pulses may not. The pin can also serve as a weak I/O pin.

Low-power CMOS 8-bit AVR on an enhanced RISC core. Most instructions take one clock, so throughput nears 1 MIPS per MHz. All 32 working registers feed the ALU directly, letting one instruction reach two registers in a single cycle. Three sleep modes are chosen in software. In Idle only the CPU stops, so SRAM, the timers, ADC, comparator and interrupt system go on working. ADC Noise Reduction leaves the ADC alone running, with the CPU and other I/O modules quiet during a conversion. Power-down shuts every function off with register contents kept, until an interrupt or a hardware reset. Flash can be reprogrammed in system over the SPI port, by an ordinary memory programmer, or by boot code on the core.
Projected data retention failure rate, from reliability qualification: well below 1 PPM across 20 years at 85 °C; 100 years at 25 °C.

Harvard architecture with separate program and data buses and a one-level pipeline: the next instruction is fetched while the current one runs, so an instruction completes every clock. The register file holds 32 x 8-bit registers with single-cycle access; an ALU operation reads two of them, computes and writes back within one clock. R26-R31 pair up as the 16-bit pointers X, Y and Z for indirect data addressing; Z also points into Flash for table lookups. Most instructions are one 16-bit word, some are 32-bit. Jumps and calls reach the whole address space.

The ALU does arithmetic, logic and bit operations between registers or between a register and a constant, in one clock. SREG reflects the result of the latest arithmetic instruction and is updated after every ALU operation. It is not saved on interrupt entry nor restored on return; software must do that.

64 I/O addresses hold control registers and peripheral data. They are reached with IN/OUT at 0x00-0x3F or as data space 0x20-0x5F (add 0x20 when using LD/ST). Registers at I/O 0x00-0x1F are bit-addressable with SBI/CBI and testable with SBIS/SBIC. Reserved bits are written as zero and reserved addresses are never written. Flags cleared by writing one may be cleared with SBI/CBI, which touch only the named bit.

The stack lives in SRAM and grows downward. PUSH decrements SP by one, a call or interrupt by two; POP increments by one, RET and RETI by two. Software must set SP above 0x60 before any call or enabled interrupt. SP is two 8-bit I/O registers, SPH (0x3E) and SPL (0x3D), reset to RAMEND.
The CPU runs from clkCPU, taken straight from the selected clock source with no internal division. Fetch and execute overlap; an internal SRAM access takes two clkCPU cycles.

Reset and each interrupt have their own vector at the bottom of program memory; the lower the address, the higher the priority, with RESET first and INT0 next. Each source has an enable bit that works together with the global I bit in SREG. Taking an interrupt clears I; setting I inside the handler allows nesting; RETI sets I again. Flag-type interrupts set a flag that hardware clears when the vector is taken, or that software clears by writing one; a flag raised while disabled waits until enabled. Level-type interrupts fire only while the condition lasts. After leaving an interrupt the core always runs one more main-program instruction before the next pending interrupt. CLI takes effect at once; the instruction after SEI always runs before any pending interrupt.

At least four clock cycles from the event to the vector, during which the program counter is pushed; the jump at the vector adds three cycles. A multi-cycle instruction finishes first. Waking from sleep adds four more cycles on top of the start-up time. Returning from an interrupt takes four cycles: the two-byte PC is popped, SP rises by two and I is set.

2, 4 or 8 Kbytes of in-system reprogrammable Flash, organised as 1024, 2048 or 4096 words of 16 bits since every instruction is 16 or 32 bits wide. The program counter is 10, 11 or 12 bits. Endurance is at least 10,000 write/erase cycles. Constant tables may sit anywhere in program memory and are read with LPM.

The data space starts with the 32 working registers (0x0000-0x001F), then 64 I/O registers (0x0020-0x005F), then 128, 256 or 512 bytes of SRAM from 0x0060 up to 0x00DF, 0x015F or 0x025F. Addressing modes: direct (whole space), indirect, indirect with displacement (63 locations from Y or Z), indirect with pre-decrement and with post-increment (X, Y, Z).

128, 256 or 512 bytes of EEPROM as a separate byte-addressed data space, endurance at least 100,000 write/erase cycles, reached through EEAR, EEDR and EECR in I/O space. Reading halts the CPU four clocks; writing halts it two. A write needs EEMPE set and then EEPE within four cycles. EEPM bits choose atomic erase-and-write (00), erase only (01) or write only (10); EEPE stays set until the operation ends and no other EEPROM access is possible meanwhile. Writing a location that was not erased first loses its data. Split erase and write lets the slow erase be done when time allows and the short write later. EEPROM timing comes from the calibrated RC oscillator, so OSCCAL must keep it in range.

Too low a VCC can corrupt EEPROM both by failing the write itself and by making the CPU execute wrongly. Holding the part in reset while the supply is short avoids it: enable the internal BOD, or use an external low-VCC reset if the BOD levels do not fit. A write already under way when reset comes completes if the supply suffices.

Clock domains: clkCPU (core, registers, stack), clkI/O (timers and most I/O; some external interrupts are detected asynchronously without it), clkFLASH (Flash interface, normally on with clkCPU), clkADC (its own domain, so CPU and I/O clocks can stop for quieter conversions) and clkPCK (fast peripheral clock from the PLL for Timer/Counter1). Sleep modes stop unused domains.

The PLL multiplies the internal 8.0 MHz RC oscillator by 8 to give a 64 MHz fast peripheral clock (PCK). With LSM set in PLLCSR the PLL takes the RC output divided by two and PCK becomes 32 MHz; LSM cannot be set while the PLL clocks the system. PCK, or a prescaled version, can clock Timer/Counter1 or, divided by four (16 MHz), the system. The PLL tracks OSCCAL changes, but PCK saturates at 85 MHz worst case if the RC is pushed above 8 MHz and the PLL then loses lock, so OSCCAL is not to be raised above 8 MHz. The PLL is on when PLLE is set or CKSEL is 0001 or 0011; PLOCK reports lock. RC oscillator and PLL both stop in Power-down.

CKSEL = 0011 selects ATtiny15 compatibility: the RC oscillator is calibrated down to 6.4 MHz, the PLL multiplies by 4 to give a 25.6 MHz PCK for Timer/Counter1, and the system clock is the 6.4 MHz divided by four, 1.6 MHz. Low speed mode (LSM) does not exist in this mode.

On wake from Power-down the selected clock source times the start-up so the oscillator is stable before code runs. From reset an extra delay, timed by the watchdog oscillator, lets the supply settle: about 4 ms is 512 watchdog cycles and 64 ms is 8K cycles. SUT and CKSEL fuses choose the delays.

CKSEL = 0000 takes the clock on CLKI (PB3). The applied frequency must not jump more than 2% between adjacent cycles; hold the part in reset across larger changes, or change speed with the system clock prescaler.
CKSEL = 0001 runs the system from the 64 MHz PLL divided by four, a nominal 16 MHz.

Gives about 8.0 MHz with no external parts; it drifts with voltage and temperature but can be trimmed closely. A factory value is loaded into OSCCAL at every reset; software may write OSCCAL for finer calibration. The watchdog oscillator still times the watchdog and the reset time-out. Parts ship with CKSEL = 0010 and CKDIV8 programmed.
A low-power oscillator, nominal 128 kHz at 3 V and 25 °C, chosen with CKSEL = 0100.

CKSEL = 0110 runs the part from a 32.768 kHz watch crystal on XTAL1/XTAL2. The pins carry internal load capacitance of 16 pF on XTAL1 and 6 pF on XTAL2; the crystal's own datasheet gives the load it needs.

XTAL1 and XTAL2 are the input and output of an inverting amplifier for a quartz crystal or ceramic resonator. C1 and C2 are always equal; their best value depends on the crystal, stray capacitance and noise. 12-22 pF is a starting point for crystals; resonators use the values their vendor specifies. CKSEL[3:1] picks one of three frequency ranges and CKSEL0 with SUT[1:0] the start-up time. The 0.4-0.9 MHz range is for resonators only.

Shipped with CKSEL = 0010, SUT = 10 and CKDIV8 programmed: the 8 MHz internal RC with the longest start-up, divided by 8, giving a 1.0 MHz system clock, slow enough for any in-system or high-voltage programmer.

CLKPR divides the system clock for every source, slowing clkI/O, clkADC, clkCPU and clkFLASH to cut power. Switching is glitch-free and no intermediate frequency exceeds the old or new setting. The ripple counter runs from the undivided clock, so the switch time cannot be predicted exactly.

With the CKOUT fuse programmed the system clock, after the prescaler, appears on CLKO (PB4) and overrides the pin's I/O role. It works with the internal RC, watchdog oscillator, PLL and external clock, but not with a crystal on XTAL1/XTAL2.

OSCCAL trims the RC oscillator. CAL7 picks the low (0) or high (1) of two overlapping ranges, so 0x7F is faster than 0x80; CAL[6:0] tunes within the range from 0x00 (slowest) to 0x7F. The oscillator times EEPROM and Flash writes: do not trim above 8.8 MHz while writing them or the write may fail.

Setting SE in MCUCR and executing SLEEP enters the mode chosen by SM[1:0]: 00 Idle, 01 ADC Noise Reduction, 10 Power-down. An enabled interrupt wakes the part; it then stalls four cycles plus the start-up time, runs the handler and resumes after SLEEP, with registers and SRAM intact. A reset during sleep restarts from the reset vector. A level interrupt used for wake-up must be held long enough.

Halts clkCPU and clkFLASH; comparator, ADC, USI, timers, watchdog and interrupts keep running, so external and internal interrupts such as timer overflow wake the part. Setting ACD switches the comparator off for lower current. An enabled ADC starts a conversion on entry.

Halts clkI/O, clkCPU and clkFLASH; the ADC, external interrupts and watchdog may run. An enabled ADC starts converting on entry. Wake sources: ADC complete, external reset, watchdog reset, brown-out reset, SPM/EEPROM ready, INT0 level interrupt, pin change.

Stops the oscillator and every generated clock; only asynchronous logic runs. Wake sources: external reset, watchdog reset or interrupt, brown-out reset, USI start condition, INT0 level interrupt, pin change.

On ATtiny25 revision E, ATtiny45 revision D, ATtiny85 revision C and later, software may turn the BOD off during Power-down so sleep current falls to the BOD-off level. Writing BODS needs a timed sequence: set BODS and BODSE together, then within four cycles set BODS with BODSE cleared; BODS is active three cycles later, SLEEP must run while it is active, and it clears itself after three cycles. The BOD returns on wake, and the wake-up then takes as long as a reset, so SUT and CKSEL must allow the bandgap to start. The revision is marked on the bottom of 8P3 and 8S2 packages and on top of 20M1.

Bits in PRR stop the clock to single peripherals. A stopped peripheral freezes and its registers cannot be read or written; its resources stay claimed, so disable it first. Clearing the bit resumes it in the same state. Useful in Active and Idle; other sleep modes stop the clocks anyway.

Use the deepest sleep that still serves. An enabled ADC stays on in every sleep mode; disable it first (the next conversion after re-enabling is an extended one). Disable an unused comparator in Idle and ADC Noise Reduction, and in every mode if it uses the internal reference. A BOD enabled by fuses and an enabled watchdog draw current in all sleep modes. The internal reference is on whenever BOD, comparator or ADC need it and must be given its start-up time after being turned on. Pins should drive no resistive load. Input buffers are off in modes where clkI/O and clkADC both stop, except those needed for wake-up; a floating input or one near VCC/2 draws excess current, so analog inputs should have their digital buffers disabled in DIDR0 at all times.

Reset loads every I/O register with its initial value and starts code at the reset vector, which must hold an RJMP to the reset routine. If no interrupt is used, program code may occupy the vector table. Ports go to their reset state at once without a clock. Once all sources release, a delay counter set by SUT and CKSEL stretches the internal reset so the supply can settle.

Four sources: power-on (VCC below VPOT), external (RESET low longer than the minimum pulse), watchdog (period expires with the watchdog enabled), brown-out (VCC below VBOT with the BOD enabled). MCUSR records which one fired.

An on-chip detector holds reset while VCC is under the POR level. Crossing it upward starts the delay counter that sets how long reset lasts after VCC rises; falling below it asserts reset again at once. RESET may be tied to VCC or held low longer from outside.
A low on RESET (if enabled) longer than the minimum width resets the part even with no clock. When the rising edge crosses VRST the delay counter starts and the part runs after tTOUT.

The BOD compares VCC with a level set by the BODLEVEL fuses, with hysteresis: VBOT+ = VBOT + VHYST/2 and VBOT- = VBOT - VHYST/2. Falling under VBOT- resets at once; rising above VBOT+ starts the delay counter and the part runs after tTOUT. A dip shorter than tBOD is not detected.
A watchdog time-out gives a reset pulse one CK long; its falling edge starts the tTOUT delay.

A bandgap reference serves the BOD and can feed the comparator or ADC. It is on only while the BOD is enabled by fuses, ACBG connects it to the comparator, or the ADC is enabled. Without the BOD, allow its start-up time after setting ACBG or enabling the ADC before using the result. Avoiding all three before Power-down keeps it off.

Runs from its own 128 kHz on-chip oscillator through a prescaler with ten periods from 2K to 1024K oscillator cycles. WDR restarts it, as do disabling it and any chip reset. On expiry without a WDR it resets the part, or it may be set to interrupt instead, handy for waking from Power-down. The WDTON fuse picks safety level 1 (starts disabled; enabling is free; disabling needs the timed sequence) or level 2 (always on; changing the period needs the timed sequence).

Level 1: write WDCE and WDE as one in a single operation (WDE must be written one whatever it held), then within four cycles write WDE and WDP as wanted with WDCE cleared. Level 2: write WDCE and WDE as one, then within four cycles write WDP with WDCE cleared; the WDE value is ignored. Clear WDRF in MCUSR before turning the watchdog off.

INT0 and PCINT[5:0] trigger even when their pins are outputs, which gives a way to raise a software interrupt. Any enabled PCINT pin that toggles fires the pin change interrupt; PCMSK selects which pins count. Pin change and INT0 low level are sensed asynchronously and can wake the part from any sleep mode; INT0 edges need clkI/O and work only in Idle. A level interrupt used to wake from Power-down must last until wake-up completes; if it goes away earlier the part still wakes but continues after SLEEP without taking the interrupt.

True read-modify-write ports: SBI/CBI change one pin's direction, value or pull-up without touching the others. Outputs sink and source symmetrically and can drive LED displays. Each pin has a selectable pull-up whose resistance does not vary with supply, and protection diodes to VCC and ground. Each port has PORTx (data), DDRx (direction) and PINx (input, read-only; writing one to a PINx bit toggles the PORTx bit). PUD in MCUCR turns off every pull-up.

DDxn = 1 makes the pin an output, 0 an input. With the pin an input, PORTxn = 1 turns on the pull-up. With it an output, PORTxn drives the level. Going between tri-state (00) and output high (11) passes through pull-up on (01) or output low (10); if the pull-up step matters, PUD disables pull-ups. Moving from pulled-up input to driven low (or back), use tri-state or output high in between.

PINxn reads the pin whatever the direction, through a latch-and-flip-flop synchroniser that delays an outside change by between ½ and 1½ system clocks. To read back a value just written to PORTx, put a NOP between the OUT and the IN; the delay is then one clock.

In Power-down the SLEEP signal clamps the Schmitt-trigger input to ground so floating or mid-level inputs draw no current. Pins enabled as external interrupts, and some alternate functions, override the clamp. A high on an asynchronous interrupt pin set for edge or any-change while that interrupt is disabled sets its flag on wake, because the clamp release looks like an edge.

Give unused pins a defined level to save current in reset, active and Idle. The internal pull-up is simplest but is off during reset; an external pull-up or pull-down covers reset too. Tying a pin straight to VCC or GND risks large current if it is ever made an output.

Peripheral functions override a pin's pull-up, direction, output value, toggle and digital-input enable through per-pin override enable and value signals. The digital input to a peripheral is taken after the Schmitt trigger and before the synchroniser; the analog path connects straight to the pad.

An 8-bit timer/counter with two independent output compare units (OCR0A, OCR0B, double-buffered in PWM modes), clear-on-compare auto-reload, glitch-free phase-correct PWM, variable PWM period, frequency generation and three interrupt sources (TOV0, OCF0A, OCF0B). It is clocked from the prescaler or from T0, and stopped when no clock is selected. TIFR holds the flags and TIMSK the masks.

CS0[2:0] picks the clock: the system clock (fastest), a prescaler tap at clk/8, /64, /256 or /1024, or T0 rising or falling edges. The prescaler runs free, so the first count after enabling comes 1 to N+1 clocks later; a prescaler reset can synchronise it to the program. T0 is sampled every system clock, adding 2.5 to 3.5 clocks of delay; each half period must exceed one system clock, so fT0 must stay under fclk_I/O/2, and under fclk_I/O/2.5 is advised to allow for oscillator tolerance. T0 must be steady for a clock when its input is switched on or off. An external clock is not prescaled.

The counter counts up, down or clears at each timer clock as WGM0[2:0] dictates. TCNT0 can be read and written whether or not the timer runs, and a CPU write wins over a count or clear. TOV0 is set according to the mode and can interrupt.

TCNT0 is compared with OCR0A and OCR0B continuously; a match sets OCF0x one timer clock later, interrupting if enabled. In PWM modes the OCR0x are double-buffered and update at TOP or BOTTOM, which keeps pulses glitch-free; in Normal and CTC the CPU writes them directly. FOC0x forces a match in non-PWM modes, changing the pin per COM0x but not setting the flag or clearing the timer. Any write to TCNT0 blocks a compare match in the next timer clock, so writing TCNT0 equal to OCR0x loses that match. Set up OC0x before making the pin an output. COM0x bits are not buffered and act at once.
Any non-zero COM0x[1:0] hands the pin to the waveform generator, but its DDR bit must still be set for the level to show. The internal OC0x register resets to 0.

WGM0 = 0: counts up through 0xFF and wraps to 0x00, setting TOV0 in the cycle the count reaches zero. TCNT0 may be written any time. Compare units can raise timed interrupts; generating waveforms this way costs too much CPU time.

WGM0 = 2: the counter clears when it matches OCR0A, which sets TOP and so the resolution. OCF0A can interrupt each period to update TOP; with no double buffering, writing an OCR0A value below TCNT0 makes the counter run to 0xFF and wrap before the next match. Toggling OC0A (COM0A = 1) gives a square wave, fastest at fclk_I/O/2 with OCR0A = 0. TOV0 sets when the count passes MAX to 0x00.

WGM0 = 3 (TOP = 0xFF) or 7 (TOP = OCR0A): single-slope count from BOTTOM to TOP, so twice the frequency of phase-correct PWM. Non-inverting (COM0x = 2) clears OC0x on match and sets it at BOTTOM; inverting (COM0x = 3) does the reverse. TOV0 sets at TOP. OCR0A = BOTTOM gives a one-clock spike each period; OCR0A = MAX holds the output steady. With WGM02 set, COM0A = 1 toggles OC0A on match for a 50% square wave up to fclk_I/O/2; OC0B has no toggle option.

WGM0 = 1 (TOP = 0xFF) or 5 (TOP = OCR0A): dual-slope count up to TOP and back down; TCNT0 holds TOP for one clock. Non-inverting mode clears OC0x on the up-count match and sets it on the down-count match. TOV0 sets at BOTTOM. Symmetric pulses suit motor control. OCR0A = BOTTOM holds the non-inverted output low and MAX holds it high. To keep symmetry about BOTTOM, OC0x may change at BOTTOM without a match: when OCR0A leaves MAX, or when the timer starts above OCR0A and misses the up-count match. With WGM02 set, COM0A = 1 toggles OC0A.

The timer is synchronous and clkT0 acts as a clock enable. TOV0 sets as the count goes from MAX to BOTTOM; OCF0x sets on the timer clock after TCNT0 equals OCR0x; in CTC and fast PWM with OCR0A as TOP, OCF0A sets and TCNT0 clears as the count passes TOP.

Setting TSM in GTCCR keeps the value written to PSR0 (and PSR1), holding the prescaler in reset so the timer can be set up without advancing; clearing TSM lets hardware clear PSR0 and the count starts. PSR0 otherwise resets the Timer/Counter0 prescaler and clears itself at once.

An 8-bit timer/counter with its own prescaler. In synchronous mode it counts from the system clock CK; with PCKE set in PLLCSR it runs asynchronously from the PLL's fast peripheral clock PCK, 64 MHz (32 MHz in low speed mode). The 14-bit prescaler offers CK or PCK divided by 1 to 16384 in powers of two, or stop; PSR1 in GTCCR resets it. Three compare registers: OCR1A drives OC1A (PB1), OCR1B drives OC1B (PB4), and OCR1C sets the clear-on-match value (TOP). Each of OCR1A and OCR1B can interrupt in normal and PWM modes. Normal mode sets TOV1 on $FF to $00; PWM mode sets it on $FF or OCR1C to $00. The inverted outputs OC1A-bar (PB0) and OC1B-bar (PB3) are only connected in PWM mode. Flags live in TIFR, masks in TIMSK, controls in TCCR1 and GTCCR.

Register writes pass through input synchronisers before reaching the counter, and TCNT1 and the flags OCF1A, OCF1B and TOV1 through output synchronisers, so their read-back lags; TCCR1, GTCCR, OCR1A, OCR1B and OCR1C read back at once. In asynchronous mode the system clock must stay below one third of PCK, since the synchroniser needs two PCK edges while the system clock is high; a faster system clock risks losing data or control values. Delays: synchronous mode ½, 1, 1 and ½ CK along the path; asynchronous mode 1-2 PCK, 1 PCK, about 1 CK and none.
Enable the PLL, wait 100 µs for it to settle, poll PLOCK until set, then set PCKE.

With PWM selected, Timer/Counter1 and OCR1C form two free-running, glitch-free 8-bit PWM generators with outputs on PB1 (OC1A) and PB4 (OC1B) and their complements on PB0 and PB3. The counter counts from $00 up to OCR1C and restarts; the OCR1C match sets TOV1 after a synchronisation delay. Clock speeds reach 64 MHz (32 MHz in low speed mode). Complementary outputs have zero non-overlap by default; the dead time generator inserts gaps. Writes to OCR1A and OCR1B go to a temporary register and latch when the count reaches OCR1C, preventing odd-length pulses; a read in between returns the newly written value. OCR1x at $00 or OCR1C holds the output steady per COM1x. TOV1 and the compare flags interrupt when enabled with global interrupts on. A lower OCR1C trades resolution for higher frequency.

With CKSEL = 0011 Timer/Counter1 and its prescaler behave as on ATtiny15; any other CKSEL code gives the normal Timer/Counter1. The clocking is always synchronous since one RC oscillator feeds both the PLL and the core. Two prescalers: 3-bit on PCK (25.6 MHz) and 10-bit on CK (1.6 MHz), offering PCK, PCK/2, PCK/4, PCK/8, CK, CK/2 up to CK/1024 in powers of two, and stop. Only OCR1A and OCR1C exist: OCR1A acts on OC1A (PB1) and can interrupt in normal and PWM modes, OCR1C sets TOP. TCCR1, GTCCR, OCR1A and OCR1C read back at once; TCNT1, OCF1A and TOV1 read back after synchronisation.

Timer/Counter1 with OCR1A forms one free-running, glitch-free 8-bit PWM on PB1 (OC1A), clocked up to 25.6 MHz. The counter runs $00 to OCR1C and restarts; the OCR1C match sets TOV1 after a synchronisation delay. OCR1A writes latch at OCR1C, and a read before the latch returns the new value. In non-PWM mode CTC1 resets the counter on the cycle after an OCR1A match; PWM1A enables PWM with the reset after an OCR1C match.

Two dead time generators, one per Timer/Counter1 PWM output, turn each PWM signal into a non-overlapping complementary pair (OC1A/OC1A-bar and OC1B/OC1B-bar) for driving external power switches. A prescaler set by DTPS1[1:0] divides the Timer/Counter1 clock, whether PCK or CK, by 1, 2, 4 or 8. An edge detector starts a 4-bit down counter loaded from DT1xH or DT1xL depending on the edge, and the rising edge of OC1x or OC1x-bar is held back until it reaches zero. The two nibbles of DT1x set the delays for the output and its complement separately, counted in prescaled dead time clock cycles, independently for each pair.

The Universal Serial Interface gives the hardware for synchronous serial links: two-wire or three-wire transfers as master or slave, a data-received interrupt, wake from Idle (and from every sleep mode in two-wire mode), and a two-wire start condition detector with interrupt. With little software it outpaces a pure software link and uses less code.

USIDR holds data in and out and is copied to USIBR for later reading; read USIDR directly without delay or data may be lost. Its MSB drives the output pin chosen by the mode through a transparent latch that moves the output change to the clock edge opposite the input sampling. Input is always sampled from DI. A 4-bit counter, readable and writable, shares USIDR's clock and interrupts on overflow; with an external clock it counts both edges. The clock comes from USCK, a Timer/Counter0 compare match, or software. In two-wire mode the clock control block can interrupt on a start condition and can hold SCL low after a start or after counter overflow to add wait states.

Matches SPI modes 0 and 1 without a hardware slave select (software can provide one). Pins DI, DO and USCK. Master and slave registers swap contents after eight USCK clocks; USIOIF marks the end. The master clocks by toggling USCK through PORTB or by writing USITC. In external clock mode 0 (USICS0 = 0) DI is sampled on rising edges and DO changes on falling edges; mode 1 uses the opposite edges. Both sides must set up data and enable outputs at least half a USCK cycle before the first sampling edge, and the counter starts at zero. Eight clock pulses, sixteen edges, overflow the counter; the overflow interrupt wakes the part from Idle. As a master the USI can clock SCK at fCK/2 by alternating two USICR writes.

Follows the TWI bus protocol but has no output slew-rate limiting and no input noise filter. Pins SCL and SDA. The master always makes the clock in software, by toggling the pin through PORTB; shifting is automatic. The clock control unit serves the slave side alone. Shifting on falling edges is the useful choice. The slave can stretch SCL low at the start or end of a transfer, so the master must check that SCL really went high. Direction is set by the protocol.

The master signals start by pulling SDA low with SCL high, via USIDR bit 7 or PORTB, with the DDR bit set. The slave's detector sets USISIF (optionally interrupting) and holds SCL low after the master's next falling edge, giving time to wake and prepare; the slave then clears the flag and resets the counter. Data is sampled on rising SCL. After eight bits of address and R/W the slave counter overflows and pulls SCL low; an unaddressed slave lets SCL go and waits for the next start. An addressed slave drives SDA low through the acknowledge clock (counter loaded with 14 before releasing SCL). Bytes then flow in one direction until a stop or repeated start. A slave that can take no more leaves the last byte unacknowledged; a reading master ends by forcing the acknowledge bit after the last byte.

Active only in two-wire mode. SDA is delayed 50 to 300 ns so SCL is sampled cleanly. The detector is asynchronous and can wake the part from Power-down, but CKSEL's oscillator start-up delay must fit the protocol's SCL hold-time limits.
SCL and SCK run at most at fCK/2, which is also the top data rate in both modes. In two-wire slave mode the clock control unit holds SCL low until the slave is ready, which can lower the real rate.

Without serial traffic the USI can serve as: a half-duplex UART in three-wire mode, more compact and faster than software alone; a stand-alone 4-bit counter with overflow interrupt (both edges count when clocked from outside); a 12-bit counter together with an 8-bit timer; an extra edge-triggered external interrupt with the counter set to F (chosen by USICS1); or a software interrupt raised by a clock strobe.

Compares AIN0 (positive) with AIN1 (negative) and sets ACO when AIN0 is higher. It has its own interrupt, triggered on output rise, fall or toggle. ACBG connects the internal 1.1 V bandgap reference to the comparator; ACD switches the comparator off. With ACME set in ADCSRB and the ADC off (ADEN = 0), MUX[1:0] in ADMUX picks ADC0-ADC3 as the negative input instead of AIN1; with ACME clear or the ADC on, AIN1 is used.

A 10-bit successive-approximation converter with a sample-and-hold. Figures given for it: 1 LSB integral non-linearity, absolute accuracy of ±2 LSB, a conversion of 65 to 260 µs, and up to 15 kSPS at full resolution. Inputs: four single-ended channels taken from Port B pins, measured from 0 V (GND) up to VCC, two differential pairs (PB3/PB4 and PB2/PB5) through a gain stage of 1x or 20x (26 dB), and an internal temperature sensor. Other features: a left-adjust option for the result, free-running or single conversions, auto-triggering from interrupt sources, a conversion-complete interrupt, a noise canceller that converts while the CPU sleeps, unipolar or bipolar differential modes and an input polarity reversal mode.

The full-scale value is VCC, the voltage on AREF (PB0), or an on-chip reference of nominally 1.1 V or 2.56 V, picked by REFS[2:0] in ADMUX; the 2.56 V reference may be filtered by a capacitor on AREF for less noise. An external reference can be used with the internal one switched off. MUX[3:0] selects the input and the differential gain. Any of ADC0-ADC3 can be a single-ended input. For differential measurements the positive input is ADC0 or ADC2 and the negative input any of ADC0-ADC3; the stage multiplies the difference by 1 or 20 before conversion, and single-ended inputs skip the gain stage.

operation.topic: ADC offset measurement, enable and result
operation.text: Connecting ADC0 or ADC2 to both sides of the gain stage converts the stage's and converter's own offset; subtracting that reading from later results taken at the same gain brings offset error below 1 LSB. The temperature sensor is MUX[3:0] = 1111 (channel ADC4). ADEN in ADCSRA turns the converter on; reference and channel choices only apply once it is on, and with ADEN clear it draws no current, so it should be off before a power-saving sleep. The 10-bit result sits right-justified in ADCH:ADCL unless ADLAR asks for left justification, in which case ADCH alone holds an 8-bit result. Read ADCL before ADCH: reading ADCL freezes both registers until ADCH is read, and a conversion that ends in between is discarded, though its interrupt still fires.

Writing 1 to ADSC starts one conversion; ADSC reads 1 until it finishes, however the conversion was started. A channel change made during a conversion waits for that conversion to end. With ADATE set, a rising edge on the source chosen by ADTS in ADCSRB resets the prescaler and starts a conversion, giving conversions at a fixed rate; an edge that comes while a conversion runs, or a trigger still high when one ends, starts nothing. The trigger's interrupt flag is set even with the interrupt disabled and must be cleared before the next event can trigger. Using the ADC's own flag (ADIF) as the trigger gives free-running mode: after a first start by ADSC, each conversion begins as the last one ends, whether or not ADIF is cleared.

For 10-bit results the converter needs a clock of 50 to 200 kHz. A faster clock trades resolution for sample rate; more than 1 MHz is not advised. A 7-bit prescaler divides the system clock by 2 to 128 (ADPS bits in ADCSRA), so any CPU clock above 100 kHz can be brought into range. It runs while ADEN is set and is held reset while ADEN is clear. A single-ended conversion started by ADSC begins on the next rising edge of the ADC clock.

A conversion takes 13 ADC clocks; the first one after ADEN is set takes 25, as the analog parts are set up. Sampling happens 1.5 clocks into a normal conversion and 13.5 clocks into the first. At the end the result is written, ADIF is set and, in single conversion mode, ADSC clears; setting ADSC again starts another conversion on the first rising ADC clock edge. With auto-triggering the prescaler is reset by the trigger, so the delay to the sample is fixed at 2 ADC clocks after the trigger edge, plus 3 CPU clocks of synchronisation. In free-running mode the next conversion starts at once and ADSC stays high.

MUX[3:0] and REFS[2:0] pass through a buffer the CPU can write at any time. The selection follows the buffer until a conversion starts, is then held for the sampling time, and follows again from the last ADC clock of the conversion. Because a conversion begins on the ADC clock edge after ADSC is written, write new values no sooner than one ADC clock after ADSC. With ADATE and ADEN both set a trigger can come at any moment; ADMUX can then be changed safely while ADATE or ADEN is clear, during a conversion at least one ADC clock after the trigger, or after a conversion before the trigger's interrupt flag is cleared, and the change applies to the following conversion. In single conversion mode, set the channel before starting, or wait for the conversion to end. In free-running mode the conversion already under way when a change is made still uses the old channel, so the first result after the change belongs to the old one. Inputs above VREF read close to 0x3FF. Discard the first result after switching the reference source.

The ADC can convert while the CPU is stopped in ADC Noise Reduction or Idle mode, away from CPU and I/O noise. Set up single conversion mode with the conversion-complete interrupt enabled and the converter idle, then enter the sleep mode; the conversion starts once the CPU halts, and its interrupt wakes the CPU. If another interrupt wakes the CPU first, that one is served and the ADC interrupt follows when the conversion ends; the CPU stays awake until the next SLEEP. Other sleep modes do not stop the ADC, so clear ADEN before entering them to avoid wasted current.

Each ADCn pin carries its pin capacitance and leakage whether or not it is selected. When selected, the source charges a 14 pF sample-and-hold capacitor through 1 to 100 kΩ of series resistance, referenced to VCC/2. Sources of about 10 kΩ or less make the sampling time negligible; a higher-impedance source needs longer to charge the capacitor, by an amount that varies widely. Low-impedance sources and slowly varying signals keep the charge transfer into the capacitor small. Content above half the ADC clock (fADC/2) aliases unpredictably, so filter it off before the input.

Keep analog traces short and over an analog ground plane, and away from fast digital lines. Do not toggle digital outputs on the port while a conversion runs. Put bypass capacitors right at the VCC and GND pins. ADC Noise Reduction mode helps most when the system clock is above 1 MHz or when the temperature sensor is read; good bypassing lessens the need for it.

A single-ended n-bit converter spans GND to VREF in 2^n steps, codes 0 to 2^n - 1. Offset error: how far the first transition (0x000 to 0x001) is from its ideal place at 0.5 LSB. Gain error: after removing offset, how far the last transition (0x3FE to 0x3FF) is from its ideal place 1.5 LSB under full scale. Integral non-linearity (INL): after removing offset and gain error, the largest distance of any transition from its ideal. Differential non-linearity (DNL): the largest departure of a code's width from 1 LSB. Quantization error: ±0.5 LSB, always. Absolute accuracy: the largest distance of any uncorrected transition from its ideal, combining all the above; ideally ±0.5 LSB. The ideal value of the other terms is 0 LSB.

Single-ended results run from 0x000 (ground) to 0x3FF (VREF less one LSB). Unipolar differential results run from 0x000 to 0x3FF; a negative difference reads as zero. The converter is unipolar by default; setting BIN in ADCSRB selects bipolar mode, where either input may be the higher and the result is two's complement from 0x200 (-512) through 0x000 to 0x1FF (+511). A unipolar signal read in bipolar mode loses one bit of range; to keep it, check the sign (ADC9 in ADCH: 1 is negative) and then convert in unipolar mode with the pair swapped by the IPR bit as needed.

The sensor is single-ended channel ADC4, selected by MUX[3:0] = 1111, and must be read against the internal 1.1 V reference in single conversion mode. Its reading rises linearly, by about 1 LSB per °C. With one calibration point at room temperature the error is typically ±10 °C; calibrating at two temperatures does better. The typical readings vary from chip to chip, so software calibration is applied with a gain k (very close to 1.0, and left out for a one-point calibration) and an offset TOS; k is found from readings at two temperatures when more accuracy is needed.

A change to REFS[2:0] during a conversion applies once it ends, and the next conversion takes 25 ADC clocks. For differential channels with gain, a VCC reference, or an AREF above VCC - 1 V, degrades accuracy. The 2.56 V internal reference needs a supply of at least 3 V. ADLAR changes the result layout at once, even in the middle of a conversion. The differential pairs are ADC0-ADC1 and ADC2-ADC3, with gain set by the MUX bits; ADC0 or ADC2 on both inputs measures offset.

An on-chip debugger using one bidirectional wire. It controls program flow, runs AVR instructions on the CPU and programs the non-volatile memories, in real time, with symbolic C or assembler debugging and unlimited software breakpoints. It emulates every on-chip function, digital and analog, except the RESET pin. With the DWEN fuse programmed and the lock bits unprogrammed, RESET becomes an open-drain bidirectional pin with its pull-up on, and carries the link to the emulator. The system clock stays whatever CKSEL selects.

A pull-up on dW/RESET, if fitted, is 10 kΩ to 20 kΩ; it may be left off. RESET tied straight to VCC does not work. Remove any capacitor on RESET and disconnect every external reset source while debugging.

Breakpoints are BREAK instructions written into Flash in place of the original instruction, which is kept and executed on resume; a BREAK can also be put in the program by hand. Each breakpoint change rewrites the Flash and so wears its data retention: parts used for debugging should not go to customers. External reset is not available while debugWIRE is on, since dW shares the RESET pin. I/O is emulated exactly at full speed; some I/O registers need care when read by the debugger with the CPU stopped. The link is asynchronous and locks to the system clock, so changing the clock in software (CLKPS) can break it, and clocks under 100 kHz can cause trouble. A programmed DWEN keeps parts of the clock system running in every sleep mode and raises sleep current, so leave it unprogrammed when not debugging.

The CPU can write its own Flash with SPM, receiving code over any interface. SPM is off until the SELFPRGEN fuse is programmed (0). Flash is written a page at a time from a temporary page buffer that SPM fills one word at a time, in any order; a page must be erased before it is written. The buffer can be filled before a page erase (which allows reading the old contents first and changing only part of a page) or between erase and write. Erase and write must both point at one and the same page.

operation.topic: SPM page erase, buffer load and page write
operation.text: Each operation is a write to SPMCSR followed by SPM within four clock cycles, with the address in Z. Page erase: SPMCSR = 00000011, page address in PCPAGE, R1:R0 ignored; the CPU halts during the erase. Buffer load: SPMCSR = 00000001, word data in R1:R0, PCWORD picks the buffer word. Each buffer word can be written once between clears; the buffer clears after a page write, on writing CTPB, and on reset, and writing the EEPROM during loading loses the buffer. Page write: SPMCSR = 00000101, page address in PCPAGE, other Z bits zero, R1:R0 ignored; the CPU halts during the write.

Z (R31:R30) holds the address. Its low bits pick the word within a page (PCWORD) and its high bits which page (PCPAGE). Erase and write are addressed separately, so software must give both the same page. LPM addresses Flash in bytes and also uses Z0. An EEPROM write blocks all SPM programming and blocks reading fuses and lock bits from software; check that EEPE in EECR is clear before writing SPMCSR.

operation.topic: Reading fuses, lock bits and signature from software
operation.text: Programmed fuse and lock bits read as 0, unprogrammed as 1. To read them, load Z, set RFLB and SELFPRGEN in SPMCSR, and execute LPM within three CPU cycles; the value lands in the LPM destination register. Z = 0x0001 returns the lock bits (LB2 in bit 1, LB1 in bit 0), 0x0000 the fuse low byte, 0x0003 the fuse high byte and 0x0002 the extended fuse byte. RFLB and SELFPRGEN clear after the read, or when no LPM follows within three cycles or no SPM within four. The device signature imprint table is read the same way with RSIG and SPMEN set and the table index in Z.

With VCC too low, a Flash write can fail and the CPU can execute instructions wrongly. Either remedy is enough: hold the part in reset while the supply is insufficient, with the internal brown-out detector when its level suits the operating voltage or an external low-VCC reset otherwise (a write under way when reset comes is completed if the supply allows); or keep the core in Power-down sleep during low VCC so it cannot write SPMCSR.

Flash accesses from the CPU are timed by the calibrated RC oscillator. RSIG reads the signature imprint table, CTPB clears its page buffer, RFLB reads fuses or lock bits (chosen by Z0), and PGWRT with SPMEN makes the next SPM within four cycles copy the buffer into the Flash page named by the high part of Z; PGWRT clears when the write completes or when no SPM follows within four cycles. Bits 7:6 of SPMCSR read zero.

Two lock bits, LB1 and LB2, unprogrammed (1) by default; only a chip erase returns them to 1. Program the fuses before the lock bits. With DWEN programmed, debugWIRE can read program memory even with lock bits set, so clear DWEN when the lock is wanted. Firmware can read the lock bits.

Three fuse bytes: extended, high and low. A programmed fuse reads 0. Fuses lock when LB1 is programmed, and a chip erase leaves them unchanged. Fuse values are latched on entering programming mode, and changes take effect on leaving it, except EESAVE, which acts as soon as it is programmed. Fuses are also latched at power-up. With RSTDISBL programmed the part can only be reprogrammed by high-voltage serial programming. SPIEN cannot be changed in SPI programming mode. DWEN must be unprogrammed for lock-bit security. The default low byte selects the internal 8 MHz RC oscillator with the longest start-up, divided by 8.

A separate signature imprint table holds three signature bytes and the oscillator calibration bytes; the rest of it is reserved. The signature can be read in serial and high-voltage programming, also when locked, and by firmware. At reset the 8 MHz calibration byte is copied into OSCCAL; in ATtiny15 compatibility mode the 6.4 MHz byte is used instead.

Flash and EEPROM are programmed over SCK, MOSI (in) and MISO (out) while RESET is held at GND, and the Programming Enable instruction must come first. A valid clock for the CKSEL setting must be present; with the internal oscillator, CLKI needs no clock. SCK low and high times must each exceed 2 CPU clocks for fck under 12 MHz, and 3 CPU clocks at 12 MHz and above. Data into the part is clocked on the rising SCK edge, data out on the falling edge. EEPROM writes in this mode erase the location automatically, so no chip erase is needed first; chip erase sets every Flash and EEPROM location to 0xFF.

Power up with RESET and SCK at 0; if SCK cannot be held low during power-up, pulse RESET high for at least tRST plus two CPU clocks after SCK is low. Wait at least 20 ms, then send Programming Enable on MOSI: when in step, the second byte (0x53) echoes back while the third is sent. Always send all four bytes; with no echo, pulse RESET and try again. Flash is loaded a byte at a time into a page with the 5 low address bits, low byte before high byte for each address, then written with Write Program Memory Page carrying the 6 high address bits. EEPROM is written a byte at a time with address and data, or a page at a time (load with the 2 low address bits, write with the 6 high bits; only loaded bytes change). Without RDY/BSY polling, wait tWD_FLASH or tWD_EEPROM before the next page or byte; talking to the interface before a Flash write ends can corrupt it. After a chip erase, 0xFF data need not be written. Read instructions return any location on MISO. End by taking RESET high; to power off, set RESET to 1 and remove VCC.

RDY/BSY returns 1 in its least significant bit while a programming operation is in progress; wait for 0 before the next instruction. Within any one page, load the low data byte before the high byte. Program-memory instructions take a word address, which may be anywhere inside its page. Unused fuse and lock bits should stay unprogrammed (1).

Flash, EEPROM, lock bits and fuses can also be programmed with 11.5-12.5 V on RESET and a 4.5-5.5 V supply, using SDI (PB0), SII (PB1), SDO (PB2) and SCI (PB3). SCI has a minimum period of 220 ns. The three Prog_enable pins (SDI, SII, SDO) are held at 0 while entering the mode.

With the Prog_enable pins at 000 and RESET and VCC at 0 V, apply 4.5-5.5 V to VCC, reaching at least 1.8 V within 20 µs; after 20-60 µs apply 11.5-12.5 V to RESET. Keep the Prog_enable pins steady for 10 µs or more once the high voltage is on, then release Prog_enable[2] (SDO) to avoid contention, and wait at least 300 µs before the first instruction. If VCC rises too slowly for that, apply the high voltage as soon as VCC reaches 0.9-1.1 V instead, and wait until VCC is within 4.5-5.5 V before the first instruction. Leave the mode by powering down or taking RESET to 0 V. To power off: SCI to 0, RESET to 1, then VCC off.

operation.topic: High-voltage programming efficiency and chip erase
operation.text: The device keeps the loaded command and address, so a command is loaded once for many locations, and the address high byte only when a new 256-word Flash or 256-byte EEPROM window starts (also for signature reads). After a chip erase, 0xFF need not be written to Flash or to EEPROM (unless EESAVE kept the EEPROM). Chip erase clears Flash, EEPROM (unless EESAVE is programmed) and the lock bits, the lock bits only once Flash is fully erased; fuses are untouched. Chip erase is needed before Flash or EEPROM is reprogrammed: load the Chip Erase command, wait after instruction 3 for SDO to go high, then load No Operation.

Flash: load Write Flash, fill its page buffer, then load the high address and program that page, waiting after instruction 3 for SDO high; repeat per page and finish with No Operation. EEPROM is likewise written a page at a time (waiting after instruction 2 for SDO high); only bytes loaded into a page are written, and there is no automatic erase in this mode. Reads load Read Flash or Read EEPROM and shift the data out on SDO. Fuses, lock bits, signature and calibration bytes have their own instruction sequences. Serial data moves on each rising SCI edge.

Two power-on reset circuits exist. The standard one is in ATtiny25 up to revision D, ATtiny45 up to revision F and ATtiny85 from revision B; the enhanced one in ATtiny25 from revision E, ATtiny45 from revision G and ATtiny85 from revision C. The revision is marked on the package: underneath on 8P3 and 8S2, on top on 20M1.

The typical curves come largely from simulation and from characterising similar devices in the same process; they are not production tested. Currents are measured with every I/O pin an input with its pull-up on and a rail-to-rail sine wave as the clock. Power-down current does not depend on the clock selected. Supply current depends mostly on voltage and frequency, and also on pin loading and switching, the code run and temperature. Parts are characterised above their tested frequency but are only guaranteed up to the frequency in the ordering code. The watchdog's own current is the gap between the power-down curves with the watchdog on and off.

In active and idle modes each module enabled through the power reduction register (PRR) adds current. The absolute figures cover three supply and clock points; the percentages scale the active or idle curves for other settings. Example: idle at 2.0 V and 1 MHz draws about 0.18 mA; enabling USI (10%), ADC (25%) and Timer0 (10%) gives about 0.261 mA.

Revisions D to F: no known errata. Revisions B and C: EEPROM reads can return bad data at low clock and low supply; avoid EEPROM when the clock is under 1 MHz and VCC under 2 V together (raise one of them). The effect depends on temperature, and the guidance holds at room temperature. Revision A was not sampled.

Revisions F and G: no known errata. Revisions D and E: the low-clock, low-supply EEPROM read fault (keep the clock at 1 MHz or more, or VCC above 2 V). Revisions B and C add three more: the PLL does not lock below 6.0 MHz, so run at 6.0 MHz or above when using it; EEPROM cannot be read from application code in lock bit mode 3, so do not use mode 3 when the code reads EEPROM; and Timer/Counter1 PWM on OC1B/XOC1B only works when COM1B[1:0] matches COM1A[1:0], so set both the same (fixed in revision D).

Revision A has the PLL, lock bit mode 3 and EEPROM read faults, plus two more. Power-down current is too high when an external clock is selected while its port pin is still an output, after an EEPROM read, or with VCC at 4.5 V or more; avoid the clock pin as an output, skip EEPROM reads where power-down current matters, and keep VCC under 4.5 V. debugWIRE loses the link when single stepping into an interrupt; disable interrupts while stepping, and debug interrupts with breakpoints inside the handler.

Revisions B and C: no known errata. Revision A: EEPROM reads can fail with a clock under 1 MHz and VCC under 2 V together; raise the clock or the supply. The effect depends on temperature, and the guidance holds at room temperature.
